questions.title: Feature that is NOT true of SGLT1
questions.question: All the following about SGLT1 are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: It is present in muscle and adipose tissue
options.C: It causes active uptake of glucose against its concentration gradient
options.D: It transports sodium down its concentration gradient

explanations.A: Correct. SGLT1 is the sodium-glucose cotransporter of the apical membrane of enterocytes (small intestine) and the renal proximal tubule; it is NOT expressed in muscle or adipose tissue, where glucose entry is instead by the facilitative GLUT4 transporter. This statement is therefore the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer. SGLT1 is genuinely insulin independent: intestinal and renal glucose uptake by SGLT1 does not require insulin, unlike GLUT4-mediated uptake in muscle and fat.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the answer. SGLT1 does move glucose against its concentration gradient. This is secondary active transport: it couples uphill glucose entry to the downhill movement of sodium.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer. SGLT1 co-transports sodium down its electrochemical gradient (maintained by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase), and this favourable sodium gradient supplies the energy that drives glucose uptake.

questions.title: Transporter that absorbs fructose
questions.question: Fructose is absorbed in the small intestine through:

explanations.A: Incorrect. SGLT1 is the sodium-dependent cotransporter for glucose and galactose, not fructose.
explanations.B: Incorrect. GLUT3 is a high-affinity glucose transporter of neurons and other cells; it does not mediate intestinal fructose absorption.
explanations.C: Correct. Fructose is taken up across the apical enterocyte membrane by GLUT5, a facilitative transporter with high specificity for fructose. Uptake is sodium-independent and follows the concentration gradient (facilitated diffusion); fructose then leaves the enterocyte basolaterally via GLUT2.
explanations.D: Incorrect. GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive glucose transporter of muscle and adipose tissue, not an intestinal fructose transporter.

questions.title: Nature of glucose uptake by muscle
questions.question: Uptake of glucose by muscles:

options.A: Occurs by an active transport mechanism

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucose enters muscle by facilitated diffusion through GLUT4, moving down its concentration gradient; it is not active transport.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Because it is facilitated diffusion, the transport itself consumes no ATP and is not energy dependent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sodium-coupled glucose uptake (via SGLT1) occurs in the intestine and kidney, not in skeletal muscle.
explanations.D: Correct. Insulin enhances glucose uptake by muscle: it triggers translocation of GLUT4 transporters from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane, increasing the number of transporters and hence the rate of facilitated glucose entry. This insulin-dependent GLUT4 recruitment is the defining feature of glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue.
